subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement best defines an ecosystem?
options: A community of plants and animals interacting with each other and the non-living physical environment
A group of the same species living in one place
Only the non-living parts of a natural area
A single, isolated food chain
questions.explain: An ecosystem is the interaction between living (biotic) organisms and the non-living (abiotic) environment in a given area.

questions.q: In a food chain, organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis are known as:
options: Producers
Primary consumers
Decomposers
Predators
questions.explain: Producers, such as green plants, convert sunlight into energy through photosynthesis and form the base of the food chain.

questions.q: What is the main role of decomposers in nutrient cycling?
options: They break down dead organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil
They produce energy directly from sunlight
They hunt and eat primary consumers
They stop nutrients from entering the soil
questions.explain: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi recycle nutrients from dead material back into the soil for plants to reuse.

questions.q: A very large-scale global ecosystem, such as tropical rainforest or hot desert, is called a:
options: Biome
Habitat
Niche
Food web
questions.explain: A biome is a large-scale global ecosystem characterised by its climate, plants and animals.

questions.q: Interdependence within an ecosystem means that:
options: The living and non-living parts rely on one another to survive and function
Each species lives completely independently of others
Only plants depend on the climate
The non-living parts have no effect on organisms
questions.explain: Biotic and abiotic components are linked, so a change to one part can affect the whole ecosystem.

questions.q: In a food web, a disease suddenly kills most of the rabbits (herbivores). What is the most likely immediate effect?
options: The number of foxes that feed on rabbits will fall
Decomposers will quickly die out
Producers will stop photosynthesising
The climate of the area will change
questions.explain: Removing a food source reduces the consumers that depend on it, showing the interdependence of a food web.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the climate of a tropical rainforest?
options: Hot and wet throughout the year
Hot days but very cold nights
Warm summers and cold winters
Cold and wet all year round
questions.explain: Rainforests have high temperatures (around 27 degrees C) and high rainfall (over 2000 mm) with little seasonal change.

questions.q: In the layered structure of a tropical rainforest, the tallest trees that poke out above the main canopy form the:
options: Emergent layer
Canopy layer
Under-canopy layer
Forest floor
questions.explain: Emergents are the tallest trees that rise above the continuous canopy to reach maximum sunlight.

questions.q: Why do many rainforest leaves have drip tips?
options: To let heavy rainwater run off quickly, preventing fungus and mould growth
To store water for the dry season
To reflect sunlight and stay cool
To trap insects for extra nutrients
questions.explain: Drip tips channel the frequent heavy rainfall off the leaf, reducing the growth of algae, fungi and bacteria.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the buttress roots found on many rainforest trees?
options: To give tall trees extra support and stability in thin soils
To store large amounts of water
To absorb sunlight for photosynthesis
To deter grazing animals
questions.explain: Large buttress roots stabilise tall trees whose roots are shallow because rainforest soils are thin and nutrient-poor near the surface.

questions.q: Which of the following is a major direct cause of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest?
options: Cattle ranching and commercial agriculture
Volcanic eruptions
Rising sea levels
Acid rain
questions.explain: Clearing land for cattle ranching and commercial farming is one of the largest causes of Amazon deforestation.

questions.q: How does large-scale deforestation contribute to climate change?
options: Fewer trees absorb less carbon dioxide, increasing the greenhouse effect
It cools the atmosphere by reducing rainfall
It increases the amount of oxygen stored in soils
It has no measurable effect on the atmosphere
questions.explain: Trees are a carbon store, so cutting and burning them releases CO2 and reduces future absorption, enhancing global warming.

questions.q: A rainforest country wants to earn income while conserving its forest. Which approach best balances development and conservation?
options: Developing ecotourism that funds conservation and provides local jobs
Clearing large areas for cattle ranches
Mining minerals across the whole region
Banning all local people from using the forest
questions.explain: Ecotourism generates income and employment while giving an economic incentive to protect the forest sustainably.

questions.q: Why is the rainforest nutrient cycle badly affected when trees are removed?
options: Most nutrients are stored in the living biomass, so removing trees strips them away
Nutrients are stored deep in the bedrock and cannot be reached
The soils are naturally very deep and fertile
Nutrients only come from rainfall, not vegetation
questions.explain: In rainforests most nutrients are held in the vegetation rather than the thin soil, so clearance quickly depletes fertility.

questions.q: A hot desert is generally defined as an area receiving how much rainfall per year?
options: Less than 250 mm
Less than 1000 mm
About 1500 mm
Over 2000 mm
questions.explain: Hot deserts are extremely arid, receiving under 250 mm of rainfall per year.

questions.q: Hot deserts are typically located in which part of the world?
options: Around 30 degrees north and south of the Equator
Directly along the Equator
At the North and South Poles
In cool coastal temperate zones
questions.explain: Sinking dry air of the subtropical high-pressure belt around 30 degrees north and south creates most hot deserts.

questions.q: How does a cactus's thick, waxy stem help it survive in a hot desert?
options: It stores water and reduces water loss from the plant
It increases the rate of photosynthesis at night
It absorbs extra rainfall from deep soils
It provides shade for other plants
questions.explain: The fleshy stem stores water while the waxy surface and small surface area limit transpiration in the heat.

questions.q: A country wants to develop its hot desert economically. Which is a realistic opportunity to pursue?
options: Extracting minerals such as copper and generating solar energy
Relying on high year-round rainfall for arable farming
Building large ski resorts on the sand dunes
Growing tropical rainforest crops without any irrigation
questions.explain: Hot deserts often hold valuable minerals and receive intense sunshine, making mining and solar power genuine development opportunities.

questions.q: Which combination of human actions is a common cause of desertification at desert margins?
options: Over-grazing, over-cultivation and removal of fuel wood
Planting trees and reducing farming
A large increase in annual rainfall
A fall in the local population
questions.explain: These pressures strip protective vegetation, exposing soil to erosion and spreading desert-like conditions.

questions.q: A community on a desert margin wants to reduce desertification. Which strategy would be most appropriate?
options: Planting trees to bind the soil and provide shade
Increasing the number of grazing animals
Removing all remaining vegetation for farming
Pumping out the groundwater to lower the water table
questions.explain: Tree planting (afforestation) holds soil together, reduces erosion and helps retain moisture, slowing desertification.
